lg.l: Informing [the confidante] about the type of separation;
[the hero] rightfully suffering when her companion speaks [of the heroine’s state];

[the confidante] saying, ‘I know’ when there is no [more] anguish; [the confidante] speaking so that [the heroine] knows;This is not clear at all. Presumably it refers to the confidante informing the heroine about some aspect of his separation. There is no poem cited that clearly corresponds to this.
the one with the fragrant forehead lamenting; [the confidante] speaking so that [the heroine] becomes amenable [to the separation];
the one with the clear jewels agreeing; [the hero and his heart] becoming confused together during the journey;
[the heroine] suffering saying, ‘The time [of his return] has come’;
while the confidante says [the heroine] has suffered, [there is] the speech of she who suffers (i.e., the heroine);
[the confidante] comforting [the heroine] – [let there be an] understanding [that these situations] are the long-distance separation,
[that] also apply to the man who comes from ‘that place’.

div.p: eṉpatu cēy iṭaip pirivām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which the long-distance separation occurs.
pirivuṇarttutaṉ mutal ākap peyarntōṉ kūṟṟīṟākac collap paṭṭaṉa cēy iṭaip pirivām eṉṟa vāṟu.
Beginning with ‘informing of the separation’ and ending with ‘the speech of the one who had returned’, those things that have been mentioned are the long-distance separation.

lg.l: We have firmly resolved to go abroadOf course puṟam literally means ‘outside’. In practice, here it refers to a place ‘outside’ of their land – whatever spatial conception that might be (village, town, country, etc.), i.e., somewhere foreign. and bring wealth

as that will bringLiterally: ‘Because of the bringing of virtue (tarutaliṉ)… we have firmly resolved (tuṇintaṉam)…’ Exactly how to understand the listed items is unclear. As translated, the first three items are treated as one group, and then the final two as another that primarily concerns the family (kiḷai). I understand it this way because it seems more sensible that at this stage, as he is already married to the heroine, there is no family that can be attained through wealth-acquisition. In an earlier stage, one could have made the argument that this might refer to the journey the hero makes to obtain the bride price, which is an established poetic situation, but it is not relevant to this late stage of the narrative. One could also translate: ‘bring virtue… and pleasure that all the family will praise’. In this understanding, pukaḻum is a peyareccam rather than an element in the enumeration. The final option is that all the listed things are the result of going off for the sake of wealth. virtue, charity, love,
and the praise and pleasure for [our] family,
O you with the garland of open flowers and shining jewels.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉ tōḻikkup pirivuṇarttiyatu.
This is the hero having informed the confidante about his separation.

lg.l: Why should I speak much [more], O loving man?

After you left,akaṉṟu is a subject-changing viṉaiyeccam. her state of separationThis is referring to her state when he has separated from her. ivaḷ pirinta an nilai could be more literally rendered as: ‘that state of separation for her’.

where her breath leaves,Should one take the final phrase, nīṅkutal uyirē, as its own sentence – ‘[Her] life is leaving’ (lit. ‘there is the departure of life’)? alas, it appeared.This poem is a warning to him. A reminder about how the heroine reacted in the past when he went away just for short trips.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi talaimakaṇilaimai kūṟic celavaḻuṅkuvittatu.
This is the confidante stopping [the hero] going by talking about the state of the heroine.

lg.l: I will say one thing, O lord.
If you desire an undertaking in the lonely distance,
where the clouds have dried up so that the ground splits open,
will the pretty, dark young woman endure that work as well?naṭai is understood as: ‘a course of action’ or ‘way of doing things’ here. It is not directly translated.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Even more than she who had resolved to come herself

so that her suffering small feet wouldThis is not explicitly conveyed in the Tamil, but it is clear that the hero is talking about something that will happen if she comes in the future, and ‘would’ conveys that in English. become red on the way
and her colour would fade like a sprout that had left the branch,

my foolish heart, who rejoicesuvakkum is taken as an imperfective peyareccam, which is identical in form to the habitual future. Were one to understand a habitual future, then the final two cīr of the poem would be their own sentence: ‘my foolish [heart] rejoices [at going through] the dense bamboo thickets with her. It is so worthy!’ The position of uvakkum strongly suggests its function as a peyareccam. [at going through]

the dense bamboo thickets with her, is so worthy.This final statement is ironic. Literally: ‘…possesses great worthiness’, but the precise meaning of the reprimand is not clear. takai is a positive attribute if standalone, so considering the context, it must be ironic. Whether it refers to the heart’s supposed ‘affection’, ‘worthiness’, ‘grace’, etc. I am not sure.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉeñciṟkuc collic celavaḻuṅkuvittatu.
This is the hero having stopped going after speaking to his heart.

lg.l: If one says, ‘a remedy?’ [she is] a remedy
and if one says, ‘a treasure?’ [she is] a treasure
– that good little daughter of the man from the rocky wilderness

with high-setpakaṭṭu can mean either ‘high’ or ‘large’. Both are plausible attributes in this context. young breasts with groups of budding beauty spots,cuṇaṅku iṉam can be split differently as cuṇaṅkiṉ am. In that case, the whole phrase would translate to: ‘pretty high-set/large breasts with beauty spots’.
wide shoulders, and a thin waist.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Once I have told her properly,neṟi as ‘the right course of action’. that this is what [you] intend,
know her stateHow she took the news, in other words. and then speak [to you],
[you] may unerringly yoke your horse to the tall chariot adorned with gold.

div.p: eṉpatu aḻuṅkātu celavu kuṟitta talaimakaṉukkut tōḻi colliyatu.
This is the confidante having spoken to the hero who had intended to go without desisting.

lg.l: I don’t know, O friend, what his heart intended.
Becoming one with a pained face
when the doe with fawn united with the stag,

not just one time[, but many], he looked [at them] intently.oru muṟai has been understood here as ‘one time/turn’ – its normal meaning – so the whole phrase oru muṟai aṉṟi refers to the hero looking a number of times besides once, i.e., looking multiple times. The idea is that seeing them united forces him to think about what he will be missing by leaving. The same idea can be expressed differently with the same words if one takes muṟai differently, as ‘way’. In that case, the whole phrase would express that he looked in a way that was not at the animals, i.e., anywhere but at the animals.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi talaimakaṭkuk kuṟippiṉāṟ pirivuṇarttiyatu.
This is the confidante having indirectly informed the heroine of [the hero’s] separation.

lg.l: Yearning for those whose minds [know] the moon-like Vedaskēḷvi can refer to either vedic knowledge, learning in general, or śruti, its Sanskrit equivalent.

and elaborate so that the benefits are obtained of the eighteen languagesIn a sense, this group of eighteen languages seems to have been an established concept by the time of the TNV, but it did not always refer to the same eighteen elements. The earliest mention of eighteen languages in a Tamil text I have found is in the Maṇimēkalai, to ‘the people of the eighteen languages’ – mūvaru pāṭai makkaḷ (28:221). No information is given about which languages or which people this specifically refers to, and there is no commentary. After that, there is no specific mention until the Tivākaram, a lexicon roughly contemporaneous with the TNV, where in section 12, verse 162, a list of eighteen languages is given under the definiendum, patiṉeṇ pāṭai (‘eighteen languages’, but where the word for ‘language’ is the Tamilised version of the Sanskrit bhāṣā). It runs: aṅkam, vaṅkam, kaliṅkam, kaucikam, cintu, cōṉakam, tirāviṭam, ciṅkalam, makatam, kōcalam, marāṭam, koṅkaṇam, tuḷuvam, cāvakam, cīṉam, kāmpōcam, aruṇam, papparam. A list of seventeen is found in Mayilainātar’s commentary to Naṉṉūl 272, possibly in the thirteenth century: ciṅkaḷam, cōṉakam, cāvakam, cīṉam, tuḷukkuṭakam, koṅkaṇam, kaṉṉaṭam, kollam, teliṅkam, kaliṅkam, vaṅkam, kaṅkam, makatam, kaṭāram, kavuṭam, kaṭuṅkucalam. This list only contains sixteen elements, with the seventeenth, Tamil, excluded. This is brought up in the context of explaining the concept of a ticai col – something like a ‘regional word’, which is essentially a word from a different linguistic area one would naturally know as a native Tamil speaker. This concept is named in the TP as one of the four classifications of words. As suggested by Chevillard, the fourfold classification from TP 391i: iyaṟcol tiricol ticaiccol vaṭacol, in that order, may have served as a tool for grading the difficulty of texts. The greater the incidence of the third three categories (different varieties of not-Tamil), the more training would be required to understand them (Chevillard 2008, 29–30). With this in mind, it makes sense that knowledge of these languages was part of some accepted idea of a syllabus – the concept of eighteen languages (or seventeen, as it may be) is mentioned multiple times in grammatical texts and knowledge of ‘foreign’ words was seemingly a marker of a highly literate individual. Perhaps this education is being alluded to in the poem and, in that case, a more apt way to construe the phrase might be: ‘the benefits of the eighteen languages in compositions of limitless erudition and great fame’. The wording of the TNV, however, leaves it open to a different interpretation. Rather than the ticaic col from the grammatical tradition, which refers purely to specific foreign words that have entered the Tamil lexicon, perhaps this TNV poem is talking about ticai moḻi (‘foreign languages’). Such a concept is implied in Tēvāram 2:92.7, where the beginning reads: teṉcol viñcu amar vaṭacol ticaimoḻi. That the verse differentiates between col, in the cases of Tamil (teṉcol) and Sanskrit (vaṭacol) and moḻi in the case of regional languages suggests a different kind of referent. Chevillard suggests an interpretation where ticai moḻi might refer to songs composed in different languages. There is, however, no explicit mention of the group of eighteen here, but there is a likelihood that the TNV was composed by a Śaiva (see \S\ref{sec:authorship}), so it may be that this poem is referring to leaving to study eighteen languages in which famous Śaiva literature was composed.
of compositions of limitless erudition and great fame,
our lover will set off and separate for other lands.

div.p: eṉpatu kalvi viḷakkuvāṉ pirivar eṉa veḷip paṭa vuṇarttiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having informed [the heroine] clearly that he will separate for the sake of further study.

lg.l: It is the duty of the young woman with beautiful jewels

to supportDepending on whether or not one takes āṟṟu-tal as transitive or intransitive, the poem can be construed differently. As currently understood, it is transitive, and the heroine is the subject and the hero the object. If intransitive, then one has to understand the syntactic relationship between the second and third lines differently. It would be the heroine’s ‘duty to endure when the hero who desired…’. the lover who is needed forOr one can understand vēṇṭiṉa kātalar as ‘the love who needs to guard’, ‘the lover who desires the guard’. the guard
that protects life on the great vast world.

div.p: eṉpatu kāttaṟkup pirivar eṉa vuṇarttiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having informed [the heroine] that he will separate to guard [the realm].

lg.l: Our beloved will leave for his manly undertaking
where he will remove the thicket of fighting swordsThis is a common way to express a melee. Cf. Pati 12.1, 31.20, 33.7 for some examples.

for the two great kings of undiminished victory.mīḷā veṉṟi is not clear. I have understood it as a victory (veṉṟi) that does not disappear (mīḷā), i.e., an ever-present or undiminished victory. There is another meaning for mīḷ-tal, common in the kiḷavi-s – ‘to return’. It is possible to translate with this meaning. One could argue that the word-order was distorted for the sake of etukai, though that is not a common feature of this collection of poems. In that case: ‘two great kings who will not return victorious’, where the implication would be that if the hero did not intervene, the result would be bad for both the great kings. Alternatively, one can translate: ‘two kings for whom victory has not returned’. Indeed one can see that the phrase has been understood both ways in the past. In his 1939 translation of the Cilappatikāram, Ramachandra Dikshitar translates the phrase mīḷā veṉṟi in 13:143 as ‘who would not return from the field victorious’ (Dikshitar 1939, 196; in this translation he understands a different headword for mīḷā veṉṟi, not given in the quotation) and then as ‘the monarch of unfailing success’ (Dikshitar 1939, 293). These are the only two times the phrase occurs in the old corpus, to the best of my knowledge. The chosen translation retains word order and makes sense in the context of two great kings going to battle. Additionally, Aṭiyārkkunallār glosses the phrase with maṭaṅkāta veṉṟiyaiyuṭaiya vēntaṉ (‘the king who possesses unbending/unsurrendering victory’) in his commentary to 13:143. It was suggested to me by Dr. Indra Manuel that this may refer to a type of battle called tumpaittiṇai from puṟapporuḷ, a ‘Major theme of a king or warrior heroically fighting against his enemy’ (TL).

div.p: eṉpatu pakai taṇippāṉ pirivar eṉa vuṇarttiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having informed [the heroine] that he will separate to appease enmity.

lg.l: Of course the lover will go to the enemiespakai micai can also refer to the abstract idea of enmity towards the king. In that case, the hero would depart to where there is enmity towards the king.
of the king with the victorious great army, won’t he?
O, one with the white lotus garland, stop suffering!

div.p: eṉpatu vēntaṟ kuṟṟuḻip pirivar eṉa vuṇarttiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having informed [the heroine] that he will separate for a royal emergency.

lg.l: ‘There is no praise at all for those men who delight in sitting at home
while abstaining from manly work day after day.’
Thinking [this], our lover left for shining wealth.
You, friend, stop your crying misery!

div.p: eṉpatu poruḷ vayiṟ pirivar eṉa vuṇarttiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having informed [the heroine] that he will separate for the sake of wealth.

lg.l: If it is said that he will not go, please say!
If [you] say he changed [his mind] and is quickly returning,māṟiṉar val varal uraippiṉ is literally: ‘If [you] say [there is] the returning of him who changed’.

there is no problem. Speak for the man who lives this way!There are other ways to construe this final line if one understands iṉṟu as ‘without’, instead of as a finite verb. The first, where, as in the translation, urai is an imperative: ‘If [you] speak about the quick return of the man who changed [his mind/course], speak for the man who lives this way without obstacles!’. The other option is to take urai as a noun and the referent of vāḻvōrkku as the heroine and those like her: ‘If [you] say… that is the speech without harm for those who live this way.’ It seems slightly unnatural to take ūṟu iṉṟu with urai as they are not placed directly next to each other, but it is certainly possible. In any case, the general idea of the poem is the same – if the confidante can tell the heroine of the hero’s quick return, then she will be ok.

div.p: eṉpatu pirivar eṉpatu kēṭṭa talaimakaḷ āṟṟāḷ āyt tōḻikkuc colliyatu.
This is the heroine, who had heard that he will separate, having spoken to the confidante after becoming unable to bear it.

lg.l: Who can separate while you, eyes overflowing with water, remain here?
[There will be] going with you whose bright forehead is swarmed by bees,
because of the honey scent that smells of
the pretty summer branches of the twisting, windingvalam can also mean ‘might’, in which case this could refer to a tree that is very windy. marā tree,
that the mountainside slopes take as an adornment.

div.p: eṉpatu āṟṟāḷ āya talaimakaṭkut tōḻi pirivu nayappac colliyatu.
This is the confidante having spoken to the heroine, who had become unable to bear [the situation], to make her agree to the separation.

lg.l: Desiring the creation of good fame,
separating from his mate and going is the duty of the lover.
Sitting at home and bearing [this] without anger
with a dignifiedōṅkiya literally means ‘to be high’. Whether the nuance is dignity or exaltation is not clear. heart because [he] went is the nature of married life.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: The man from the land with the high mountains with flowing waterfalls,
as though seeing the moon rise over the sea
– he is like the sun, O friend –
and my large bamboo arms are like the neriñci plant.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ pirivuṭaṉ paṭṭatu.
This is the heroine having agreed to [the hero’s] separation.

lg.l: Thinking of the crossroads in the difficult desert
and of the great cool northern wind that comes

because [you] separated,This causal construction ending in pirinteṉa has been translated faithfully, but perhaps ‘when’ might be more apt than ‘because’. It is not clear whether the idea is that the wind actually comes because he has left, whether it is painful because he has left, or simply that this will occur once he has left. we shall suffer.

div.p: eṉpatu pirivuṭaṉ paṭṭa talaimakaṭalaimakaṟkuc colliyatu.
This is the heroine, who had agreed to [his] separation, having spoken to the hero.

lg.l: Having urged on the swift horsesOne can either understand kaṭum pari as a metonymic reference to the horses, as in the translation, or as literally: ‘Now we have driven the tall chariot at a great speed’. of the tall chariot
whose nature is like the wind, gone through the pālai wilderness,
and completed our work, let us now return!
The loneliness of the girl with a body like gold is very great.

div.p: eṉpatu pirintu cellun talaimakaṉ ṟērp pākaṟkuc colliyatu.
This is the hero, who had separated [from the heroine] and left, having spoken to the charioteer.

lg.l: You did not stay [with her] there in that place.
Now rise here in this place! Live, my heart!
For the sake of the wealth [we] resolved upon making,

the dark kajal eyes of the girl of humble words weep.The syntax of the last two and a half lines can be construed differently. As understood in the translation, they are a standalone phrase that tells the precondition for the state of the heroine, but there is no finite verb. The other options would be to either connect poruḷ vayiṉāṉ to the root imperative in which case the poem would read: ‘rise here, for the sake of the wealth…’, or to understand it as a kind of predicate for īṇṭi ivaṇ and understand vayiṉāṉ literally instead of as a locative postposition. This would translate to: ‘Rise here, in this way, in the place of the wealth [we] resolved to make…’.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉ iṭaic curattut talaimakaḷai niṉainta neñciṉait teḷittuc ceṉṟatu.
This is the hero having gone on after clarifying [the matter] with his heart, who was thinking of the heroine in the middle of the desert.

lg.l: I was careless thinking, ‘He won’t go.’

And he stayed behindoḻintaṉar can also be understood as ‘he left aside’ or ‘he declined’. In that case the line would read: ‘he declined [to invite me] saying…’. In both cases the hero does not ask the heroine to join him on his journey thinking she will refuse. Whether or not he has actually left for his trip at the time when this is spoken is not clear. It is also not clear in KT 43, though in PK 300 he has left (see apparatus). thinking, ‘She won’t agree.’

O [one] with the good, beautiful kajal eyes, my heart is afflicted.Presumably this means that he has now left, having previously stayed without inviting her, but this is not certain.This final phrase could also be translated: ‘My heart, my good beautiful kajal eyes are afflicted’. The chosen translation stays closer to KT 43 (provided in the apparatus), where the final line deals with the state of the heroine’s heart.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉ aṟiyāmaṟ pirinta viṭattut talaimakaḷ āṟṟātu colliyatu.
This is the heroine having spoken, being unable to bear it during the separation without knowledge of the hero.

lg.l: Having become fragrant,viraii (‘having become fragrant’) can have as its subject: all of the flowers, the glory lily alone, or the piṭavu and kōṭal flowers. Based on its position, I understand the last option that doesn’t require understanding a subject-changing absolutive. It makes little difference to the meaning of the poems or the image. they are foolish:
as the piṭavu, the kōṭal, and the Malabar glory lily

along with the laburnum that makes garlands,maṭava tārīṉ can be split differently as maṭavat’ ār īṉ. In this case the laburnum would be ‘abundantly blossoming’. maṭavatu would then require either just one of the plants to be its referent, or the forest. The KT source reads maṭava, and I think that is the intention of the author. appear,
the forest takes on the rainy season.

O, our eyes do indeed take on water.The speech situation is not so clear. If the speaker has already stated the flowers are foolish, then why have they become disconsolate? Perhaps one ought to understand maṭava as an unmarked instrumental: ‘Because they are foolish, as they appeared, the forest took [the appearance of] the rainy season’. Then the final line is a comparison to the flowers – an implicit statement that their tears are also foolish.

div.p: eṉpatu paruvavaravu kaṇṭāṟṟāḷ āyatu.
This is [the heroine] having become disconsolate on seeing the season [of his arrival] coming.

lg.l: Live, O friend! Like him, has it forgotten our life?
Since the man from the land of forests,
where parakeets are chased away from the millet
by the beating of pestles in the houses, left,
my dark beauty – it also left.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Small bleak evening! Small bleak evening!
After the cool wind blows like a fiery chill,
and you take away the redness,Or ‘and you take on redness’ for cekkar koṇṭa. Either way, the phrase alludes to the sun setting.

small bleak evening,The peyareccam phrase ,… koṇṭa ciṟu puṉ mālai, is not accurately rendered, as the main poetic play here is the repetition of the phrase ciṟu puṉ mālai, and this was the closest and most natural way to retain that. you come to us daily.
You never go to his hilly land!

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ āṟṟāmaikkut tōḻi yāṟṟāḷ āyiṟṟu.
This is the confidante having become disconsolate because the heroine cannot bear [the separation].

lg.l: They say it is not pleasing, that difficult desert,
where the stomachs of the mothers of the young men
commanded by the taṇṇumaiA type of war drum. drum being suitably beaten

by the pulaiyaṉ to say, ‘You men in a line, go,’This type of imperative ending in -mō normally has a polite nuance – ‘please go’. This phrase is alluding to some kind of war formation, so this may be because it is the appropriate form of address from their own general. grow pained.
What of the road he travels, O friend?

div.p: eṉpatu āṟṟāḷ āya tōḻikkāṟṟuval eṉpatu paṭac colliyatu.
This is [the heroine] having spoken to the confidante, who had become disconsolate, to be told something comforting.

lg.l: So that, as scandal and great blame spread, [our] goodness was ruined

and pallor spread on [our] suffering small foreheads –The two infinitive clauses can both be understood as co-ordinated temporal clauses, so: ‘While… spread (…tūṟṟa), and while [our] goodness… spread (…pāya)’. Alternatively, they can both be understood as resultative: ‘So that… spread, and so that [our] goodness… spread’. The chosen translation does not require co-ordination.
are the hills in his land even crueller
than that man who did this to us? O friend,

not even one [cloud] has appearedtōṉṟā is a homophonous form. It can either be analysed as a negative absolutive, as done in the translation; as a negative neuter plural; or as a contracted form of the negative neuter singular. All of the options result in a similar meaning of the poem – no rain clouds appear – but the finite forms require two clauses in the final sentence in the translation to be split into two finite sentences. and the rains have failed.In the phrase maḻai maṟantaṉa, both words can be translated differently: maḻai as either ‘rain’ or ‘cloud’, and maṟa-ttal as either ‘to forget’ or ‘to fail’. In AN 241.7 and Tēvāram 7:55.2, almost the same phrase refers to the rains failing, so I have followed that here, though either ‘clouds’ or ‘rain’ would refer to the same thing – the rainy season. Seeing as the point of comparison in the poem is between the cruelty of the hero and cruelty of the hills, taking maṟa-ttal as ‘to fail’ is more sensible. Then, the idea is that the hills have prevented the rain clouds from reaching the heroine. Because the hero had promised to return before the rains, the heroine now blames the hills for also preventing his arrival. If one takes the verb as ‘to forget’, it is the cruelty of the clouds, not of the hills, that is emphasised.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi yāṟṟuvippāṉ ṟalaimakaṉai iyaṟ paḻittatu.
This is the confidante having belittled the nature of the hero to comfort [the heroine].

lg.l: Although [my] arms speak of his crueltyThese first two lines can be interpreted slightly differently, as a direct response to the confidante’s rebuke of the hero’s in the previous poem. In this case, rather than the heroine’s arms telling the cruelty of the man, the confidante would be the subject of kūṟu-tal: ‘Although [you] spoke of his cruelty [whereby] my arms became emaciated…’. by becoming emaciated
so that the bangles slip and fall down,toṭi naṭant iḻiya literally translates to: ‘so that bangles walk and fall down’. there is no cruelty
on the part of the man from the land with good mountains, O friend.
He has not separated from my heart and

he has not forbidden [my] glances at his hills.This could work two ways. Either the final two lines enforce the fact that the heroine bears no ill will towards the hero, or they can work as a final lament. For the first situation, see the translation presented, where the sight of his land calms the heroine, for the second: ‘He does not chase away [my distress] with the sight of his hill’, i.e., nothing can cure my pain apart from his return. The TPn reading, tam kuṟai, to which Dr. Indra Manuel suggested emending, works nicely: ‘and he does not discard his pleading look’. In this case, the poem is the heroine justifying the hero’s behaviour by saying she still knows he loves her.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ ataṉukkāṟṟāḷ āy moḻintatu.

This is the heroine having spoken after becoming disconsolate on account of that [separation].Alternatively, the heroine is unable to endure the confidante’s criticism of the hero from the previous poem, which pushes her to praise him in this one.

lg.l: BecauseThe -eṉa on urutteṉa can either carry a causal or comparative sense, and I think both retain the same basic understanding of the line. I understand a causal function, as the flowers are blooming because the clouds have actually started to rain; it is just that the rains are not the monsoon, when the plants should normally flower. The comparative sense would imply the burden that the clouds carry is the monsoon rain and that it has not yet been shed and that this was simply a shower. dark clouds full of water had weakened and issued forth their burden,How to take uruttal is not totally clear. The emendation by UVC makes good sense – for the rain cloud to shed their burden – but the poem is still understandable without it. A similar meaning is arrived at in the translation presented. Another option would be to take uruttal in its meaning of ‘to mature’, in which case: ‘the clouds full of water weakened and matured [with regard to] their burden [of rain]’.
having seen without understanding the new cool rains,Cf. KT 382.4 for vampu referring to a specific type of rain left over from the previous rainy season.

[she] suffers, thinking, ‘This is the rainy season’.I have taken varuntum as an habitual future, rather than an imperfective aspect peyareccam, so I split the poem into two sentences. There is no difference to the sense of the poem if one translates it as a peyareccam: ‘[and] even more than her who suffers, thinking...’ [And] even more than her,
all the great cool jasmine, which budded in clusters of buds

like the teeth of the brilliant smile on her mouth, possess a bright smile.As I understand it, the point of the comparative phrase in the last two and a half lines is to say that the jasmine flowers have now overtaken her smile. That has, in turn, only served to increase her suffering (as the jasmine budding is a marker of the monsoon season). The confidante is pointing out the folly on both their parts, and gently mocking both the heroine and the jasmine for being misled.

div.p: eṉpatu paruvam aṉṟeṉa vāṟṟuvittatu.
This is [the confidante] having comforted [the heroine] by saying, ‘It is not the season [of his return].’

lg.l: Even though [you] think ofThis must carry some sort of negative connotation for the concessive to make sense. The reference to the ‘long way’ may suggest the heroine is thinking primarily of the difficulty and danger of the road. the heavy rain in the forest that the rains did indeed make,The -ē on kār-ē is a bit ambiguous. Is this to state that the forest only exists thanks to the rainy season?
and the long way, where pollen sits atop the kōpam cactus,

the chariot of that most worthy manneṭum takai is understood as a synonym of perum takai. One can find it used as such a number of times in the PN (cf. PN 272.7 and 296.5, for example). One could also take both neṭum and takai as properties of the chariot, in which case: ‘the tall, worthy chariot has come so that…’. has come
so that the heart rejoices and the birds rise up.

div.p: eṉpatu tēr varavu kūṟi yāṟṟuvittatu.
This is [the confidante] having comforted [the heroine] by talking about [the hero’s] chariot coming.

lg.l: Amongst the jasmine in the clearings,See the critical notes to illam for a brief discussion on the meaning of kollai. interspersedmiṭainta can also mean: ‘to be crowded/full’ or ‘to be set close’. One could then translate this line: ‘Amongst the jasmine in clearings close to the houses’, which amounts to much the same as the suggested translation. between the houses,
in the confusing dark evening, whenever [she] hears
the sorrowful āmpal fluteThis could also be the name of a specific melody, and presumably has some sort of romantic connotation. of the cowherds with many cows,
does the pitiful one, our beloved, become disturbed?

div.p: eṉpatu viṉai muṭittu mīḷvāṉeñciṟkuc colliyatu.
This is the one who was returning having spoken to his heart after completing his task.

lg.l: O great cloud full of rain, stop your cruelkaṭum can mean either ‘fast’ or ‘quick’ and both work in this context. If the hero pleads with the cloud to stop its journey, it is so he can reach the heroine before it and thereby prevent her distress on seeing the rainy season arrive before him. Taking it as ‘cruel’, the effect of the cloud’s appearance on the heroine is emphasised. journey,
as the girl with eyes overflowing with tears will become lonely,
thinking the lover has become one who won’t return.

div.p: eṉpatu mukilukkuc colliyatu.
This is [the hero] having spoken to a cloud.

lg.l: Please mount the chariot, O charioteer!

‘Seeing the rains,The agent of kār kaṇṭu can also be the heroine, in which case one would attach it to the verb pula-ttal. In this case, the heroine would see the rains, think the hero was prolonging his encampment, and become aggrieved. my lover has prolonged his encampment.’
Thinking [this], she is one who stays [at home], becoming aggrieved at us.nam pulant’ uṟaivōḷ can also mean: ‘she is one who remains aggrieved at us’.

Let us go right this moment,ippoḻutu aḷavaiyiṉ pukuka nām literally translates to: ‘We must go there within the measure of this moment!’ I.e., ‘We must go there right now!’ so that [she] sees [us].The hero could also be the agent of kāṇa, in which case he would be keen to get going so he could see her. Considering KT 250, upon which this poem is loosely modelled, and the fact that this poem primarily deals with the hero’s concern for the heroine’s well-being (or possible anger with him, if one is a bit less generous), it is more likely that she would be the one to see him. The idea is that sight of him will put her mind at rest.

div.p: eṉpatu tērp pākaṟkuc colliyatu.
This is [the hero] having spoken to the charioteer.

lg.l: Because you revealed the coming of the lover,

O conchThe implicit comparison is between the conch and the moon. Its curling rays give away that this is the case. A common attribute of a conch is that it is rightward-spiralling (cf. PN 225.12, 283.7). with encircling rays and a spiral face,

may you live longThe village watch sounds a conch when the hero arrives, so praising it is another way to express joy at his return. onuḻai here functions as a locative postposition. this world of blooming expanse!

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi caṅkiṉai vāḻttiyatu.
This is the confidante having praised the conch.
eṉpatu talaimakaṭkut tōḻi colliyatu.
This is the confidante having spoken to the heroine.

lg.l: But for [my] body remaining there with difficulty,
would my heart, which had been united with your innocent glance,
have been able to bear separation from you?

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṭkut talaimakaṉ colliyatu. 24.
This is the hero having spoken to the heroine.

standOff.note: Cf. TP25n: ōtal pakaiyē tūtivai pirivē ||
Cf. IA45: pukaḻuṅ koṭumaiyuṅ kiḻavōṉ mēṉa

Both C1 and Cām mean the same – they are neuter singular obliques of the root uri- (‘to have the right’), used adverbially. uritiṉiṉ clearly became the standard form after a point, but there is no grammatical reason to discount uritaṉiṉ. There are other examples of this variant (see AN 186.17: uritiṉiṉ in Irākavaiyaṅkār’s 1923 edition; uritaṉiṉ in Wilden’s upcoming edition, currently only published online at ), including another in this text (TNV 18, poem 7), also emended to uritiṉiṉ by UVC. My impression is that such variants were normalised in the majority of cases. As it is a perfectly valid form transmitted by C1 and it is documented elsewhere, I retain the ‘variant’ form.

The pattern in this cūttiram is clear: each situation enumerated ends in a verbal noun finishing in -al. There is no direct parallel I have found for this phrase or for this situation in another grammatical treatise or koḷu/kiḷavi, so I assume UVC emended here for that reason. This pattern, however, is not a constant through the rest of the TNV. There are multiple cūttiram-s that use different syntactic constructions to describe situations. In TNV 20, for example, all but the final situation in the enumeration end in a verbal noun in -al. The final ends in the noun kiḷavi, a synonym for kūṟṟu in this context. One sees it used in a similar context in the second layer of the commentary: peyarntōṉ kūṟṟu (‘the speech of the one who returned’). Since the reading in Cām seems to be pure conjecture and there is some evidence that it is unnecessary, the C1 reading is maintained. The remaining doubt I have is that kūṟṟu is always preceded by an agent in the TNV (and somewhat curiously, it only appears from TNV 23 onwards and then with some regularity, though I do not think this is meaningful). One can construe the phrase with nōvāḷ as the agent, though there are other possibilities (see the footnotes to the translation). Even if one interprets it differently, I would argue the C1 reading is still perfectly comprehensible, though it becomes less convincing.
Cf. AV170.1: eṉporuṭ pirivuṇar tēntiḻaik keṉṟal
Cf. IAC39, p. 222: tōḻi talaimakaṇilaimai talaimakaṟkuc colliyataṟkuc ceyyuḷ
This same poem in the AV exemplifies a different situation – talaivaṉ pōkkuṭaṉ paṭutal (‘the hero agreeing to elope’).

Cf. AV62.1: ōtaṟkup paṭartal
Cf. AV62.2: aruṭṭaku kāval
Cf. AV62.2: tūtiṟ kakaṟal
Cf. IAC39, p. 215: vēntaṟkuṟṟuḻip piriyaluṟun talaimakaṉ tōḻiyāl talaimakaṭkup pirivuṇarttuvittup piriyum.
Cf. AV62.3: utavik kēkal
Cf. IAC39, p. 222: poruṭkup piriyaluṟṟa talaimakaṉ tōḻiyāl talaimakaṭkup pirivu uṇarttuvittaṟku ceyyuḷ
Cf. AV62.3: nitiṟ kikattal
Cf. IAC39, p. 222: atu kēṭṭu āṟṟāttaṉmaiyaḷāya talaimakaḷ tōḻikkuc colliyataṟkuc ceyyuḷ
Cf. AV170.5: pūṅkuḻai yiraṅkal
Cf. AV169.2: pirivuṭaṉ paṭuttal
Cf. IAC39, p. 218: vēntarkkuṟṟuḻic ceṉṟu viṉaimuṟṟi miḷvāṉ tērppākaṟkuc colliyataṟkuc ceyyuḷ

Reading Cām - the peyareccam niṉainta aligns much better with the action of the poem, where, in the first two lines, the hero pleads with his heart to stop thinking of the heroine and get on with the task at hand – making money. C1 keeps the hero as the agent of niṉai-tal, in which case the hero would be the one who thought about the heroine before clarifying matters with his heart. This is possible, but since the koḷu-s of the TNV generally reflect the action of their respective poems very closely, and since the emendation required is so minor, I follow UVC and print niṉainta.
Cf. AV170.5: pūṅkuḻai yiraṅkal
This AV situation was cited for an earlier TNV situation as well. The AVC quotes the source material for this TNV poem (KT 43) to exemplify this, which is why it is cited again as a parallel.

Cf. IAC53, p. 253: ivai piriviṭaip paruvaṅkaṇṭu āṟṟāḷāyayiṉa talaimakaḷai itu paruvamaṉṟu; eṉṉai? avar poyyuraiyārākalāṉ; ituvum vampu, vampiṉaip paruvam eṉṟu tammaṭamaiyāṟ piṭavuṅ kōṭaluṅ koṉṟaiyum mayaṅkip pūttaṉaveṉṟu vaṟpuṟuttāḷām.
Cf. AV170.8: paruvaṅkaṇṭu perumakaḷ pulampal

In the IAC, it is the confidante who says this to console the heroine, whereas here it is the heroine’s lament. Even though the speech is just a summary of what is found in NA 99, which is quoted as a source of the poem, it is still included as it is impossible to know whether the author drew from the NA poem or the prose summary.

Presumably the emendation in Cām was made on the strength of the koḷu to the previous poem and the general pattern of the koḷu-s to the illustrative verses provided in the commentary to this cūttiram. There are other instances of koḷu-s ending in āyiṟṟu, though, which UVC let be. Indeed, in the koḷu to TNV 22, poem 16, we find the exact same final phrase: āṟṟāḷ āyiṟṟu. Both seem perfectly acceptable in this context, and reflect the non-standardised nature of the koḷu-s to the TNV, so I retain C1’s reading.
Cf. IAC53, p. 252: talaimakaṉṟaṉṉai aṉpilaṉ koṭiyaṉeṉavum ittoṭakkattaṉavellāñ colliyum āṟṟuvikkum.
Cf. AV170.11: piṇaiviḻi yāṟṟal
Cf. IAC39, p. 224: piriviṭai melintu āṟṟāḷākiya talaimakaḷaip paruvam vantateṉṟu vaṟpuṟuppa vaṉpuṟaiyetiraḻintu colliyataṟkuc ceyyuḷ
Cf. IAC53, p. 252: avaṟṟiṟ paruvavaraviṉkaṇ āṟṟāḷāṉa talaimakaḷai āṟṟuvittaṟkup paṭaittumoḻintu paruvamaṉṟeṉṟataṟkuc ceyyuḷ
Cf. AV170.9: ikuḷaivam peṉṟal
Cf. IAC53, p. 253: piriviṭaiyāṟṟāḷākiya talaimakaḷait tōḻi avar kuṟitta paruvam vantatākaliṉ avarum poyyār varuvar eṉṟu vaṟpuṟuttiyatu.
Cf. AV170.10–11: avartū tākivan taṭantatip poḻuteṉat | tuṇaivi cāṟṟal
Cf. AV170.12: avaṉavaṇ pulampal
Cf. AV170.12–14: avaṉvaruṅ kālaip | pākaṉ ṟaṉṉoṭum mēkan taṉṉoṭum | cōkaṅ koṇṭavaṉ collal
Cf. IAC55, p. 258: caṅkam paṭakam paṭac caṅkiṉai vāḻttiyataṟkuc ceyyuḷ
Cf. AV170.14–15: pāṅki | valampuri kēṭṭavaṉ varavaṟi vuṟuttal
Cf. AV170.17: niṉaittamai ceppal

Cf. TK268: kuṉṟaṅ kiṭaiyuṅ kaṭantumar kūṟu nitikoṇarntu | miṉṟaṅ kiṭainummai yumvantu mēvuva ṉampalañcēr | maṉṟaṅ kiṭaimaru tēkampam vāñciya maṉṉapoṉṉaic | ceṉṟaṅ kiṭaikoṇṭu vāṭā vakaiceppu tēmoḻiyē ||
Both C1 and C2 etc., are imperfective first person forms. There are no exact parallels that would suggest one reading is preferable to the other, so I revert to C1.
One could make sense of the reading in C1, where the verb is in the third person honorific, but here it is far more natural to read the second person, considering this is a direct address.
Cf. TK335.2–3: kāṉak kaṭañcelvar kātala reṉṉak katirmulaikaḷ | māṉak kaṉakan tarumalark kaṇkaṇmut tamvaḷarkkum
Cf. Cilap12.2: āṟucel varuttatuc cīraṭi civappa
UVC records varuttañ cīraṭi as a variant in his 1920 edition of the Cilappatikāram.

The C1 reading is possible, where kuru would be an adjective meaning ‘brilliant’ (see Kali 101.5). kuṟu makaḷ, however, is an exceptionally well-attested phrase to refer to the heroine. In addition, no known KT 71 MS reports the C1 reading. Thus, this edition follows UVC.

Cf. IAC35, p. 209: ōtaṟkup piriyumeṉpatu kaṟpāṉ piriyumeṉpataṉṟu, paṇṭē kuravarkaḷāṟ kaṟpikkap paṭṭuk kaṟṟāṉ aṟam poruḷiṉpam vīṭupeṟukaḷ nutaliya nūlkaḷellām; iṉip paratēcaṅkaḷiṉum avai vallār uḷareṉiṟkāṇpaleṉṟum, vallārkaḷ uḷvaḻic ceṉṟu taṉ ñāṉam mēṟpaṭuttu avarkaḷ ñāṉaṅ kīḻppaṭuttaṟkup piriyumeṉakkoḷka.
Cf. TK309.2–4: nammai kalvi celvītaru meṉpatukoṇ | ṭōtaluṟ ṟāruṟ ṟuṇartaluṟ ṟārcellaṉ mallaḻaṟkāṉ | pōtaluṟ ṟārniṉ puṇarmulai yuṟṟa puravalarē ||
Cf. PK244.1–2 (IAC36, p. 213): tēkkiya teṇtirai munnī rirunilan tītakalak | kākkiya celvatu kātalit tāraṉpar

I do not see a clear reason why UVC emended here. Both readings keep the same meaning, at least as I understand the poem, and there are no clear parallels for either of them. They are both grammatically sound, so I retain the C1 reading.
Cf. Cilap13.143; 26.32: miḷā veṉṟi vēntaṉ
Cf. TP72n.11–13: vāḷvāyt | tiruperu vēntar tāmuñ cuṟṟamu | moruvaru moḻiyāt tokainilaik kaṇṇum
Cf. PK245.1–2 (IAC37, p. 214): tākkiya pōrvaya vēnta riruvarkkuñ cantiṭainiṉ | ṟākkiya celvatu kātalit tārnamar
Cf. TK314.1–2: mikaitaṇit taṟkari tāmiru vēntarvem pōrmiṭainta | pakaitaṇit taṟkup paṭartaluṟ ṟārnamar
Cf. PK246.1–2 (IAC39, p. 215): vārār muraciṉ viraicēr malarmuṭi maṉṉavaṟkāyc | cērār muṉaimicaic cēṟaluṟ ṟārnamar
Cf. PK247.1–2 (IAC39, p. 216): kaṉṉavi ṟōṇmaṉṉaṉ ṟemmuṉai mēṟkala vāraivelvāṉ | viṉṉavi ṟōḷaṉpar celvar
This poem is not printed in UVC’s first edition (1937).
Cf. PK268.1–2 (IAC39, p. 222): illā rirumaiyu naṉmaiyey tāreṉ ṟirunitikkuk | kallār curañcelva tēniṉain tārnamar
Cf. TK333.1–2: vaṟiyā rirumai yaṟiyā reṉamaṉṟu mānitikku | neṟiyā raruñcurañ cellaluṟ ṟārnamar

Both varal and varavu are nominal derivations from vā-/varu-tal and neither is particularly common directly preceding verbs of speech like we find in this poem (‘tell about his coming’). In general, I do not see a clear syntactic pattern where the object of description ought to be the nominal derivation ending in -vu as opposed to in -al. varavu uraittal is a phrase found in the koḷu-s to the TK and PPVM (see TK 156 and PPVM 2.14, for example), which may have convinced UVC to emend. There is one text-internal example of a nominal derivation in -vu preceding uraittal, in TNV 20.1: ayal varaivu uraittal (‘[the confidante] talking about marriage [offers from] the neighbourhood’). I am not convinced that this is meaningful. Due to the structure of the cūttiram, where verbal nouns ending in -al end a speech situation, the author might not have wanted to use one apart from in that function, to save confusion. There is, however, some evidence in support of C1 from the Caṅkam corpus. In some editions of the AN, and one documented manuscript, poem 35.15 reads: iṉṟu varal uraimō (‘tell [me] of [his] coming today’; Irākavaiyaṅkār 1923). It seems this was a valid and recorded construction, so since it is reported by C1, I retain it.
One does not expect any consonant gemination after an enclitic ē.

The C2, KT, etc. reading makes perfect sense – the -um on niṉṉoṭum is co-ordinating with the hero, i.e., the two of them going together. This is not, however, necessary, so this edition retains the C1 reading. Probably incidentally, the same phrase, as found in C1, appears as the final two cīr-s in PN 265.
Cf. PN18.16: nallicai niṟuttal vēṇṭiṉum
This poem is addressed to the heroine, according to the koḷu, so C1’s reading does not make sense. It would require this to be addressed to the hero, as kātala is a vocative of the masculine kātalaṉ.

Both readings are perfectly sensible, and neither has clear parallels in a prior text, so I am not sure why UVC emended. Perhaps he thought it was more appropriate for the heroine to sit at home with a sad, weakened heart (olkiya uḷḷam), though it seems equally plausible in the context of the poem that she ought to feel a sense of dignity and even pride – her husband is doing himself (and by extension, her) proud, and she is performing her duty.

In terms of meaning, there is little difference between C1pc and C2 etc,. I preserve C1pc not because I argue it is the ‘original’ reading, but because I want to retain evidence of what I believe is a strand of transmission. The C1pc readings are reported in KT manuscripts and editions (see Wilden 2010). Confusingly, UVC prints ñāyi raṉaiyaṉ in his 1937 KT edition, published in the same year as his TNV edition, so it is not obvious where his TNV reading – raṉaiyaṉeṉ – came from.
The standard spelling for this plant is printed by UVC, but as the C1 reading is included in the TL as an alternate spelling, it is retained and printed here.
Cf. PK255.1–2 (IAC39, p. 218): veṉṟē kaḷittacev vēṉeṭu māṟaṉviṇ ṭārmuṉaimēṟ | ceṉṟē viṉaimuṟṟi mīṇṭaṉam
Cf. KT11.3–4: āṅkē | yeḻuviṉi vāḻiyeṉ ṉeñcē
Cf. AN19.1–2: aṉṟava ḷoḻintaṉṟu milaiyē vantunaṉi | varuntiṉai vāḻiye ṉeñcē
Cf. TK342: poṉṉaṇi yīṭṭiya vōṭṭaru neñcamip poṅkuveṅkā | ṉiṉṉaṇi niṟku miteṉṉeṉpa tēyimai yōriṟaiñcum | maṉṉaṇi tillai vaḷanaka raṉṉavaṉ ṉannaṭaiyāḷ | miṉṉaṇi nuṇṇiṭaik kōporuṭ kōnī viraikiṉṟatē ||

C1 and the emended reading in Cām are formulaic addresses for the heart, and thus are regularly interchanged. Both of the source poems read vāḻiye(ṉ) ṉeñcē in the majority of editions and MSS, so I assume UVC edited on that basis. The C1 reading is reported in Wilden (2010). Since this is such a common variant, I find it impossible to judge what version of either KT 11 or AN 19 the other might have followed, if that was even his intention. In the absence of any secure evidence, I revert to the manuscript.
Cf. KT43: celvā rallareṉ ṟiyāṉikaḻn taṉaṉē | yīvā ḷallaḷeṉ ṟavarikaḻn taṉarē | yāyiṭai yirupē rāṇmai ceyta pūca | ṉallarāk katuvi yāṅke | ṉalla ṉeñca malamalak kuṟumē ||

Cf. PK304 (IAC52, p. 250): cellā ravareṉ ṟiyāṉikaḻn tēṉcurañ cellattaṉka | ṇollā ḷavaḷeṉ ṟavarikaḻn tārmaṟ ṟivaiyiraṇṭuṅ | kollā rayiṟpaṭaik kōṉeṭu māṟaṉ kuḷantaiveṉṟa | villāṉ pakaipō leṉatuḷḷan taṉṉai melivikkumē ||

Cf. TK340: piriyā reṉavikaḻn tēṉmuṉṉam yāṉpiṉṉai yeṟpiriyiṉ | tariyā ḷeṉavikaḻn tārmaṉṉar tāntakkaṉ vēḷvimikka | eriyā reḻilaḻik kummeḻi lampalat tōṉevarkkum | ariyā ṉaruḷilar pōlaṉṉa veṉṉai yaḻivittatē ||

The source evidence here is very convincing in favour of Cām’s reading. For one, ikaḻ-tal (‘to be negligent’) makes better sense here than ika-ttal (‘to transgress’). For KT 43, there are no recorded witnesses that transmit the same reading as C1. As a very similar phrase is found in the first lines of not just the PK but also the TK, it is safe to conclude that by the time of the TNV, this had become an established trope in the poetic situation. There is no doubt that these were the reference points of the TNV, so it is reasonable to expect it to follow the pattern.
Cf. KT66: maṭava maṉṟa taṭavunilaik koṉṟai | kalpiṟaṅ kattañ ceṉṟōr kūṟiya | paruvam vārā vaḷavai neritarak | kompucēr koṭiyiṇa rūḻtta | vampa māriyaik kāreṉa matittē ||
Cf. NA99.8–10: tērvila | piṭavuṅ koṉṟaiyuṅ kōṭalu | maṭava vākaliṉ malarntaṉa palavē ||
Cf. PK306.3–4 (IAC53, p. 252): poṉṉē | maṭakkoṉṟai vampiṉaik kāreṉa veṇṇi malarntaṉavē ||

Cf. TK324: teḷitaraṟ kāreṉac cīraṉañ ciṟṟam palattaṭiyēṉ | kaḷitarak kārmiṭaṟ ṟōṭai māṭakkaṇ ṇārmuḻavan | tuḷitaraṟ kāreṉa vārttaṉa vārppat tokkuṉ kuḻalpōṉ | ṟaḷitarak kāntaḷum pāntaḷaip pārit talarntaṉavē ||
Cf. TK319.2–4: viruppiṉa mēvacceṉ ṟārkkuñceṉ ṟalkuṅkol vīḻpaṉivāy | neruppiṉa mēyneṭu māleḻi ṟōṉṟacceṉ ṟāṅkuniṉṟa | poruppiṉa mēṟit tamiyaraip pārkkum puyaliṉamē ||
Cf. TK321.3–4: iṭumpaṉi pāritta vāparan teṅkumvaiyañ | caramaṉṟi vāṉṟaru mēlokku mikka tamiyarukkē ||

It is not clear why UVC chose to emend here. C1 makes good sense (to me, at least). paṉippu is the abstract noun of the strong root paṉi-ttal ‘to become cold’, so ‘a chill’ in this context, or something similar. This works perfectly well as a comparison. Reading paṉi (‘dew’, ‘coldness’) reads well, but I question the necessity of deviating from the manuscript. There are no parallels for this phrase I have found, and the TPn reading agrees with C1.

nalaṉ aḻintu and nalaṉ iḻantu both make sense and produce a similar meaning: either the heroine’s goodness is ruined, as in C1, or lost in the case of Cām. There is one Caṅkam parallel I have found for C1 in Kali 134.7, but many for the Cām reading. It is perfectly possible that both C1 and TPn are the result of a similar scribal error, but unlikely that the two would independently arrive at the same uncommon, but sensible, collocation, so I retain C1’s reading.

There is very little difference in meaning here between C1 and Cām, etc., but Cām’s reading makes for a cleaner syntax. The ummai particle in C1 – kuṉṟu-um – is slightly awkward. If one takes it as a kind of eccavummai, then it is a bit redundant with the comparative avariṉum. Its distributive function makes more sense – ‘all of the hills’ – but it is still unnecessary. We also find kuṉṟam in the final line of the next poem. I think here there is enough reason to move away from a grammatically inelegant C1 reading and follow Cām, a reading also supported by TPn. There are no reported variants in any edition of the TPn that I have found.

Unlike in the above case, I think a strong argument can be made against TPn. maḻai maṟa-ttal (‘rain/clouds failed [to come]’) has parallels in AN 241.7, where the heroine complains of the rains failing when her lover is away, and Tēvāram 7:55.2. maḻai maṟai-tal has only one Caṅkam quasi-parallel I have found in AiN 252.2, where clouds hide huts. There, one finds maṟai-ttal, the transitive form. If one were to take Cām’s reading, it could be understood two ways: either the hills or the clouds are the subject of maṟai-tal (‘to be hidden’). If the clouds, then the general sense of the poem remains the same – the rain clouds are hidden by the cruel hills. If the hills are the subject, then they are hidden behind the clouds, and the heroine is unable to remind herself of her lover with their sight. We see this idea in the next poem, but it seems unlikely here as it would give agency to the clouds, where the comparison in the poem is between the hills and the hero.
Cf. PK309.3–4 (IAC53, p. 253): varuntal pirinta tuḷaṅkoḷicē | raṭiyār kaḻalā raṇukavan tārtta takalvicumpē ||
Cf. PK311.3–4 (IAC53, p. 254): varuntaṉ maṭantai varuvarnaṅ kātalar vāṉatirak | kuruntam poruntiveṇ mullaika ḷīṉṟaṉa kūreyiṟē ||
Cf. TK349: pāviyai vellum paricillai yēmukil pāvaiyañcīr | āviyai vellak kaṟukkiṉṟa pōḻtatti ṉampalattuk | kāviyai vellu miṭaṟṟō ṉaruḷiṟ katumeṉappōy | mēviya māniti yōṭaṉpar tērvantu mēviṉatē ||
Cf. NA371.7–9: aḻaṟuṭaṅ kiṉaḷē yāyiḻai yataṉetir | kuḻaṟuṭaṅ kiṉarē kōvalar | aḻaṅkukura lurumiṉ kaṅku lāṉē ||

Perhaps UVC was influenced by the phrase illamoṭu miṭainta in NA 376, though he does not provide a footnote, so it is difficult to know for sure. There, illam refers to an Illam tree, whose flowers are used in a chaplet to which are also attached (miṭainta) other flowers. This makes for a sensible reading in this poem: the jasmine are found in the clearings full of illam trees. The C1 reading, though, is supported by an independent witness – Iḷampūraṇār’s commentary – and one can make sense of it. The main issue here, which I suspect may have also played a role in UVC’s decision to emend, is that one would not expect a kollai, which refers to an area of dry shrubland bushes which is to be burned to create arable land for millet-fields, to be found amongst the houses of a village. One could argue the pastoral image of the cowherd’s flute-playing makes more sense in the fields outside of the inhabited area of a settlement as well. According to unattested entries in the TL, a kollai can refer to a garden or a yard attached to a house. The usage may provide evidence for a semantic shift away from a millet-field, to garden or yard. With supporting evidence for C1, which I believe UVC was unaware of, as he made no note of it in his edition where he would for other quotations in TP commentaries, I revert back to C1. There is a possibility UVC took illam as house, but then there is no clear rationale for the emendation.
Cf. PK263.3–4 (IAC39, p. 220): kaṇtē raḻintu kalaṅku mavaṭaṉ kaṭinakarkkeṉ | ṟiṇṭēr celavaṉṟi muṉcellal vāḻi ceḻumukilē ||
Cf. TK329.3–4: paḻaṅkaṇ ṭaruñcelvi cīrnakarkkeṉ | runtē ritaṉmuṉ vaḻaṅkēl muḻaṅkēl vaḷamukilē ||
Cf. AN29.21–24: māṇviṉaik | kuṭampāṇ ṭoḻintamai mallatai | maṭaṅkeḻu neñca niṉṉuḻai yatuvē ||
Cf. KT250.3–6: mālai vārā vaḷavaik kāliyaṟ | kaṭumāk kaṭavumati pāka neṭunīrp | porukayaṉ muraṇiya vuṇkaṭ | ṭeritīṅ kiḷavi terumara luyavē ||
Cf. PK255.2–4 (IAC39, p. 218): kāruñ ciṟitiruṇṭa | tiṉṟē pukumvaṇṇa mūrkatiṇ tēriḷa vañciyeṉṉa | niṉṟē vaṇaṅku nuṭaṅkiṭai yēḻai neṭunakarkkē ||
Cf. PK260.2–4 (IAC39, p. 220): muṉṉukatēr | neymmā ṇayiṉeṭu māṟa ṉiṟaipuṉaṟ kūṭalaṉṉa | maimmāṇ kuḻalāḷ maramaṉṟu vāṇiṭai vārpuyalē ||
Cf. TK328.2: tuṉaintu perukuka tēr

I do not think UVC’s emendation is necessary, and there is a textual parallel/source that supports C1. He may have thought aḷavai (‘measure’) was redundant following ippoḻutu (‘[at] this time’), or perhaps he expected aḷavai to appear with a definite time frame, which he did not think ippoḻutu conveyed. I think this is a rhetorical feature of the poem, which denotes a temporal limit and emphasises urgency. We find aḷavai used in exactly this way in KT 250, upon which this poem seems loosely modelled. In lines 3–4: mālai vārā aḷavai… kaṭavumati pāka (‘drive, charioteer… before evening comes’). I therefore print C1.
Cf. PK318.2–4 (IAC55, p. 258): mālkaṭaṟ ṟōṉṟiṉai maṇṇaḷanta | nīṉiṟa vaṇṇaṉu mēntiṉaṉ ṟammu ṉiṟampuraitīm | pāṉiṟa veṇcaṅkam yārniṉṉiṉ mikka paṭimaiyarē ||
Cf. IAC55, p. 258: purivaḷai vāṉkōṭu puttēḷō ṭotti | tiruvaḷar mārpaṉu mēntiṉaṉ ṟammuṉ | ṉuruvam puraiyuniṉ kēḻ ||
I can only imagine this was a copying error by UVC when he made C2. The two forms are identical in meaning and function, and ka and ta look similar.

In this poetic situation – ‘the praising of the conch’ – one would expect the conch to be explicitly named, as is done in the source poems and Cām’s emendation. Additionally, the attribute curi mukam (‘spiral face’) is one commonly associated with a conch. They have rightward spirals (cf. puri vaḷai at the beginning of the anonymous IAC poem quoted as a source). It is probable that a scribe read cūḻ katir, which is a natural attribute of the moon, and consciously or unconsciously replaced paṇilam (‘conch’) with matiyam (‘moon’). Praising the conch is not a common poetic situation, so a scribe may not have expected this image (though it is explicitly stated in the koḷu). If one were to read C1, it would be possible to understand the moon as a kind of ākupeyar, where a conch is the actual referent but its moon-like qualities allow the metaphor. This feels abstruse for this collection of poems and, considering: the source material, that this is a praise poem, that there is no parallel for the metaphor in C1, and that the change to matiyam is more likely than the other way around, I follow UVC.

In lieu of an apparatus, the full transcription of the poem as found in Cām is provided. The text in the paper copy of the MS and print editions is identical. It is not clear how UVC arrived at this text. Perhaps C1 has deteriorated in the years since he acquired it.

Cf. PK307 (IAC53, p. 252): pūritta meṉmulai yāyaṉṟu pūlantaip pōrmalainta | vērit toṭaiyal vicaya caritaṉviṇ ṭōykollimēṉ | mūrik kaḷiṟu muṉintukai yeṟṟa muḻaṅkukoṇṭaṉ | mārikku mullaiyiṉ vāynaka vēnī varuntuvatē ||

Instinctively, UVC’s emendation seems preferable. It feels natural for a rain cloud to shed (uku-ttal) its burden. UVC presumably felt so, and changed the reading. This is not, however, a verb that I have found used with any regularity in the vicinity of any word for cloud. Therefore I have chosen to print C1, as I think one can make sense of it and it would be an unlikely scribal mistake to be replicated. For notes on its meaning, see the footnotes to the translation.
